L25: # Bounded VC-dimension implies the Erdős–Rado sunflower conjecture
L26: Gennian Ge School of Mathematical Sciences, Capital Normal University, Beijing, China. Email: gnge@zju.edu.cn. Gennian Ge is supported by the National Key Research and Development Program of China under Grant 2025YFC3409900, the National Natural Science Foundation of China under Grant 12231014, and Beijing Scholars Program.    Jian Wang School of Mathematics, Sichuan University, Chengdu, China. Email: wangjianmath01@scu.edu.cn.
L27: Jian Wang is supported by National Natural Science Foundation of China Grant no. 12471316.    Zixiang Xu School of Mathematical Sciences, Zhejiang University, Hangzhou, China. Email: zixiangxu@zju.edu.cn.    Xiaochen Zhao School of Mathematical Sciences, Capital Normal University, Beijing, China. Email: 2250501013@cnu.edu.cn.
L28: ###### Abstract
L29: 
L30: The Erdős–Rado sunflower conjecture asserts that, for every fixed integer $r\geq 3$, there is a constant $K(r)$ such that every $\ell$-uniform family with more than $K(r)^{\ell}$ members contains an $r$-sunflower. We prove this conjecture for families of bounded VC-dimension.
L31: ## 1 Introduction
L32: A collection of distinct sets $H_{1},\ldots,H_{r}$ is an $r$-sunflower, or a $\Delta$-system, if every two of its members have the same intersection. Thus there is a set $C$, called the kernel, such that $H_{i}\cap H_{j}=C$ whenever $i\neq j$, the sets $H_{i}\setminus C$ are the petals and are pairwise disjoint. A family is $\ell$-bounded if each of its members has size at most $\ell$, and is $\ell$-uniform if each of its members has size exactly $\ell$.
L33: This simple intersection pattern is one of the fundamental configurations in extremal set theory. For integers $r\geq 3$ and $\ell\geq 1$, let $f_{r}(\ell)$ be the maximum size of an $\ell$-uniform family containing no $r$-sunflower.
L34: In 1960, Erdős and Rado [【12†11】] proved the classical sunflower lemma $f_{r}(\ell)\leq(r-1)^{\ell}\ell!$, which have become standard reduction tools across combinatorics and theoretical computer science [【13†1】, 【14†8】, 【15†9】, 【16†12】, 【17†18】, 【18†23】, 【19†24】, 【20†25】, 【21†27】, 【22†28】, 【23†29】], and the remarkable persistence of the problem reflects the difficulty of forcing even this rigid local structure from a purely global hypothesis on the size of a family.
L35: Erdős and Rado [【12†11】] also conjectured that the factorial term can be removed: there should be a constant $K(r)$, depending only on $r$, for which
L36: 
L37:  | $$f_{r}(\ell)\leq K(r)^{\ell}.$$  |
L38: The conjecture has been one of the favorite open problems of Erdős [【24†10】], which remains open in general and also stands as one of the most important problem in the field of extremal combinatorics [【25†6】]. In a major breakthrough, Alweiss, Lovett, Wu, and Zhang [【26†3】] obtained a bound of the form $\bigl(Cr^{3}\log\ell\log\log\ell\bigr)^{\ell}$, Bell, Chueluecha, and Warnke [【27†5】] subsequently sharpened the best general estimate to $\bigl(Cr\log\ell\bigr)^{\ell}$.
L39: These advances introduced and refined the spread viewpoint that now plays a central role in extremal set theory [【28†7】, 【29†16】, 【30†17】, 【31†19】, 【32†20】, 【33†21】, 【34†22】, 【35†34】].
L40: For a set system $\mathcal{H}$, a set $D$ is shattered if $\{H\cap D:H\in\mathcal{H}\}=2^{D}$, and the VC-dimension $\operatorname{VC}(\mathcal{H})$ is the largest size of such a set. This parameter measures the complexity of the traces of $\mathcal{H}$. Its basic counting consequence is the Sauer–Shelah lemma [【36†30】, 【37†31】, 【38†33】], which gives the largest size of a set systems with bounded VC-dimension.
L41: Bounded VC-dimension has repeatedly made difficult extremal conjectures accessible. Fox, Pach, and Suk [【39†13】] initiated the study of the Erdős–Hajnal conjecture in this setting. Nguyen, Scott, and Seymour [【40†26】] subsequently resolved the bounded-VC case completely: for every fixed $d$, there is a constant $c=c(d)>0$ such that every $n$-vertex graph with VC-dimension at most $d$ contains a clique or an independent set of size at least $n^{c}$, also see a recent improvement on the exponent [【41†32】].
L42: Fox, Pach, and Suk [【42†14】] also proved the Schur–Erdős prediction $r(k;m)=2^{\Theta_{k}(m)}$ for edge-colorings whose monochromatic neighborhood systems have bounded VC-dimension.
L43: The sunflower problem under bounded VC-dimension was first studied by Fox, Pach, and Suk [【43†15】]. They proved that an $\ell$-uniform family $\mathcal{H}$ with $\operatorname{VC}(\mathcal{H})\leq d$ contains an $r$-sunflower whenever $\lvert\mathcal{H}\rvert\geq 2^{10\ell(dr)^{2\log^{*}\ell}}$.
L44: Balogh, Bernshteyn, Delcourt, Ferber, and Pham [【44†4】] later obtained the substantially sharper sufficient condition $\lvert\mathcal{H}\rvert>\bigl(Cr(\log d+\log^{*}\ell)\bigr)^{\ell}$ for an absolute constant $C$, and also determined the sharp bound when $d=1$. For general fixed $d$, however, the exponential base still depends on $\ell$. Our main result removes this final dependence.
L45: ###### Theorem 1.1.
L46: 
L47: Let $d\geq 1$, $r\geq 2$, and $\ell\geq 1$. If $\mathcal{H}$ is an $\ell$-bounded set system with $\operatorname{VC}(\mathcal{H})\leq d$ and no $r$-sunflower, then
L48: 
L49:  | $$\lvert\mathcal{H}\rvert\leq\sum_{k=0}^{\ell}(50dr)^{k}<2(50dr)^{\ell}.$$  |
L50: 
L51: In particular, every $\ell$-uniform set system $\mathcal{H}$ with $\operatorname{VC}(\mathcal{H})\leq d$ and $\lvert\mathcal{H}\rvert>(50dr)^{\ell}$ contains an $r$-sunflower.
L52: 
L53: ## 2 Proof of main result
L54: ### 2.1 Notation and Tools
L55: 
L56: For a family $\mathcal{G}$ on a ground set $X$ and $T\subseteq X$, write
L57: 
L58:  | $$d_{\mathcal{G}}(T)=\lvert\{G\in\mathcal{G}:T\subseteq G\}\rvert.$$  |
L59: Thus $d_{\mathcal{G}}(T)$ is the number of members of $\mathcal{G}$ that contain $T$. For $E\subseteq X$, the family $\{G\cap E:G\in\mathcal{G}\}$ is called the trace of $\mathcal{G}$ on $E$. We write $\nu(\mathcal{G})$ for the matching number of $\mathcal{G}$, that is, the maximum number of pairwise disjoint members in $\mathcal{G}$.
L60: Let $0<q<1$. A nonempty family $\mathcal{G}$ is $q$-spread if $d_{\mathcal{G}}(T)\leq q^{\lvert T\rvert}\lvert\mathcal{G}\rvert$ for every nonempty $T\subseteq X$. In other words, the proportion of members containing any prescribed set $T$ is at most $q^{\lvert T\rvert}$. If $G$ is chosen uniformly from $\mathcal{G}$, meaning that each member is chosen with probability $\frac{1}{\lvert\mathcal{G}\rvert}$, we write
L61:  | $$\mu_{x}=\mathbb{P}(x\in G)=\frac{d_{\mathcal{G}}(\{x\})}{\lvert\mathcal{G}\rvert}.$$  |
L62: 
L63: Thus $\mu_{x}$ is simply the probability that a random member contains $x$. For a $q$-spread family, the case $T=\{x\}$ gives $\mu_{x}\leq q$.
L64: 
L65: We use the following standard form of the Sauer–Shelah lemma [【36†30】, 【37†31】, 【38†33】].
L66: ###### Lemma 2.1.
L67: 
L68: Let $\mathcal{G}$ be a set system on $X$ with $\operatorname{VC}(\mathcal{G})\leq d$, and let $E\subseteq X$ have size $m\geq d\geq 1$. Then
L69: 
L70:  | $$\lvert\{G\cap E:G\in\mathcal{G}\}\rvert\leq\sum_{i=0}^{d}\binom{m}{i}\leq\left(\frac{em}{d}\right)^{d}.$$  |
L71: 
L72: We shall use some facts about entropy. If a discrete random variable $Y$ takes only finitely many values, its support is the set of its possible values, namely
L73: 
L74:  | $$\operatorname{supp}(Y)=\{y:\mathbb{P}(Y=y)>0\}.$$  |
L75: Writing $p_{y}=\mathbb{P}(Y=y)$, the entropy of $Y$ is defined as
L76: 
L77:  | $$H(Y)=\sum_{y\in\operatorname{supp}(Y)}p_{y}\log\frac{1}{p_{y}}.$$  |
L78: 
L79: Thus entropy is the average of $\log\frac{1}{p_{y}}$, where each possible value $y$ is given its probability $p_{y}$. Unless a base is displayed explicitly, all logarithms in the proof are natural. The entropy cannot exceed the logarithm of the number of values that the random variable can take. Indeed, by the concavity of the logarithm,
L80:  | $$H(Y)\leq\log\left(\sum_{y\in\operatorname{supp}(Y)}p_{y}\frac{1}{p_{y}}\right)=\log\lvert\operatorname{supp}(Y)\rvert.$$  |  | (1)
L81: 
L82: We also use the following standard Caro–Wei bound for the independence number of a graph, see [【45†2】]. Here $\alpha(J)$ denotes the largest size of an independent set in $J$, and $\deg_{J}(v)$ denotes the degree of a vertex $v$.
L83: ###### Lemma 2.2.
L84: 
L85: If $J$ is a graph with $N$ vertices and $e(J)$ edges, then
L86: 
L87:  | $$\alpha(J)\geq\sum_{v\in V(J)}\frac{1}{\deg_{J}(v)+1}\geq\frac{N^{2}}{N+2e(J)}.$$  |
